title: Budget 2026: The two big decisions Chancellor John Healey has to make
description: "It is tough," John Healey admitted to me earlier this month when I asked him if there had been too much doom-mongering?"Conflicts, uncertainty, drivi
body: "It is tough," John Healey admitted to me earlier this month when I asked him if there had been too much doom-mongering?"Conflicts, uncertainty, driving up inflation, driving up interest rates. But we've got great strengths. We've got good reasons to be confident about the future of Britain," he insisted.The new scheme to try and help young people get on the property ladder, announced on Saturday, was aimed at boosting confidence in the economy.But the chancellor is now facing two big decisions before his inaugural Budget on 28 October.Firstly, about the longevity of the economic pressures caused by the Iran War, and then about how to sustain a modest but notable uptick in economic spirits, through yet more global turbulence.In his first weeks as chancellor the oil price fell as low as $75 a barrel while the yield - the effective interest rate - on 10-year government bonds was 4.9%.Just over two months later oil has largely traded above $100 and the 10-year yield is at around 5.4%. It is the ultimate double whammy for a chancellor facing his first Budget.Yet there is something unusual about this energy shock. It could quickly reverse, as illustrated earlier in the summer when assumptions about a deescalation in the US Iran conflict led to sharp falls in energy prices and yields.In New York this week both President Trump and his Iranian counterpart President Pezeshkian suggested November's US midterm elections were connected to when the war might end.The Iranians would wait until after the elections to seek peace because the war's impact on the cost of living - particularly soaring diesel costs - could damage him electorally, the US president told the UN General Assembly.The Iranian president said his nation "didn't want it to get to the midterms".Both sides in this war are feeling the economic squeeze of conflict. The 3 November vote is six days after the Budget. No one could rely on there being a settlement by then, but it is plausible.So the Budget tax, spend and borrowing forecasts could be based on a prolonged conflict, which is actually on the cusp of ending, or even already ended. The chancellor has to therefore decide whether to plan for the worst, and make some painful permanent tax and spend decisions, or buy some time.One option is to let borrowing take some of the strain, by tolerating a reduction in the £24bn of headroom - room for manoeuvre against its self-imposed borrowing rules - left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves.This year's headroom will be judged in three years rather than four, so there is some rationale as to why a smaller number over a closer target might be appropriate.And while higher inflation means higher interest costs, it also means higher cash tax receipts, at a time when thresholds continue to be frozen.There is a second consideration. The hopeful optimism "vibes" strategy of the Burnham administration appears to have had some impact.The longest running UK consumer confidence survey has hit a two-year high. Among younger people it has not been this high since before Brexit.Some data companies call it a "Burnham bounce", although the weather and World Cup were also factors.There is evidence, more mixed, that business optimism has also perked up in recent months, possibly because of earlier falls in energy prices, though this has been clouded by anticipation of possible tax rises. Business group, the Institute of Directors said this was despite, rather than because of, the new government.While no one should get too carried away with these turnarounds, they do stand in contrast to the admitted mistake of the Starmer government in talking up consumer pain, two years ago. The question for the chancellor is whether better consumer and business spirits can be reconciled with the need for a "challenging" Budget?Indeed, it's important to determine how much of the summer global bond market shock is solely down to the impact of the Iran war and how much is more structural.Governments are facing new and intense competition in bond markets from the world's biggest AI businesses. In addition, the UK has had recent, prominent political and economic uncertainty.Right now the bond markets are like a pack of wolves stalking red deer, probing for weaknesses."At times like this you don't want to be at the back of the herd," said one very senior former Treasury adviser. In response, the Treasury has pointed to the UK having the highest growth and the fastest falling borrowing of the major G7 countries so far this year and our overall energy prices starting to decouple from high and volatile gas prices.However, the IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva this week dismissed the idea that advanced nations could pause their fiscal homework, while the Gulf situation calmed."Bring debt levels down, make fiscal consolidation as a priority… it is impossible to stress strongly enough how critical it is to get the courage to take the steps that are necessary," Georgieva told me, acknowledging the UK's "fairly consistent, credible" plans.Then there is the curious conundrum of British productivity. Last year, the government's official forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) downgraded the UK's productivity peformance, leading to a notable hit to the public finances.Now the UK's productivity record has been upgraded materially by the Office for National Statistics, although this is because of fewer hours worked. There could therefore be an argument to reverse some of that downgrade.Separately, the new chair of the OBR Jonathan Haskel is known for his argument that official statistics understate investment in intangibles like software and data. His latest research suggests AI-related investment is already visible in US productivity figures, and he has long been optimistic about tech's impact on the future.While it seems unlikely that such factors will make it into the OBR's calculations next month, there is a real debate here. Officially, however, part of the job at the Budget is to identify cuts to fund the Defence Investment Plan, inherited from Sir Keir. That's before funding the additional move to 3% of GDP and a new social care system. Even a promise of less welfare spending looks like being built on an upfront investment in jobs for young people.One change from last year is that so far, the government has parked the "pitch-rolling" with a silence that would rival the Trappist monks.Instead, policy announcements are strategically timed such as the "Your First Home" scheme just as the Labour party conference got underway. We can expect to hear plenty more as the Budget nears.

schema.headline: Budget 2026: The two big decisions Chancellor John Healey has to make

title: Nor'easter storm brings coastal flooding, as New York and New Jersey declare emergency
description: Figure caption, Watch: Huge waves pummel northeast US as storm barrels throughByKwasi Gyamfi AsieduUpdated 5 hours agoTens of millions of people acros
body: Figure caption, Watch: Huge waves pummel northeast US as storm barrels throughByKwasi Gyamfi AsieduUpdated 5 hours agoTens of millions of people across the north-eastern US are in the path of a powerful storm bringing coastal flooding, power cuts, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events.The so-called nor'easter is bringing "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston on Saturday, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said. States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, both of which faced a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds are forecast from Virginia to Maine.In Brooklyn, a man was killed by a falling tree, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Surf City, New Jersey, was among coastal communities floodedThe nor'easter has caused widespread power cuts. More than 100,000 households, nearly all in the northeast US, have lost electricity, according to tracker PowerOutage. The Federal Aviation Administration recommended air passengers check with airlines about their flight status. More than 2,400 flights have been delayed and another 1,199 grounded, according to FlightAware.Saturday's full moon is projected to worsen coastal flooding. Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan on Saturday."I urge all New Jerseyans to take this storm seriously, stay alert and follow local guidance," Governor Mikie Sherrill said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhoodNWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses." In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power lines."Don't travel if you don't have to," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater."In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved the last game in their series against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in coastal parts of New JerseyImage source, ReutersImage caption, Flights have been delayed or cancelled due to the stormA professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled. The Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, will not go ahead.Ed Sheeran's Boston concert was also among events called off due to the weather.Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Waves pounded the coast in Massachusetts

schema.headline: Nor'easter storm brings coastal flooding, as New York and New Jersey declare emergency

title: Iranian minister says only negotiation can end conflict after Trump rejects Hormuz deal
description: Only a "negotiated solution" can end the conflict between the US and Iran, Tehran's foreign minister has said, after President Donald Trump publicly r
body: Only a "negotiated solution" can end the conflict between the US and Iran, Tehran's foreign minister has said, after President Donald Trump publicly rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.Trump told reporters at the White House that Iran's proposal was not "acceptable" and that Tehran wanted to make a deal to open the strait to commercial shipping  within seven days because "they're losing so badly".In a post on Telegram, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's rejection, but said Iran would wait for a "definitive" official US response.He said the president had made contradictory statements in the past.Araghchi said the conditions to open the strait were the same that had been included in a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the US and Iran that was signed in June.Iran said it had raised reopening the strait and ending hostilities during negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this past week.The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February."I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it, causing massive rises in global oil prices and steep fuel cost increases for consumers.Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently".He continued: "We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them."Separately, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, who travelled to New York for the UN general assembly, told the BBC's US news partner CBS that "distrust created by this war needs to be overcome" in order for talks to be successful. He said the Iranians were open to talks on implementing the MOU in stages in order to end the impasse, but that the "US needs to show it does not intend to overthrow our government".Pezeshkian said Trump had "tore up" the MOU when the US resumed its bombing campaign, adding: "If we don't abide by what we have written down, can we really resolve it by dialogue?"He was also asked about Iran's new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who was injured in the US strike which killed his father in February and has not been seen in public since. Reports have claimed he suffered serious injuries to his legs and face.Pezeshkian said he had met the supreme leader on two occasions, telling CBS he had "no specific ongoing health issues or challenges" and had been well enough to hold seven hours of talks.Oman, which has been acting as a mediator between the US and Iran, called for all parties to continue having open dialogue to resolve the crisis.Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi, told the UN General Debate that "all parties" should cooperate with Oman in efforts to safeguard navigation in the strategic waterway.Trump's rejection of Iran's proposal was backed by US ambassador to Nato Matthew Whitaker.Speaking to Fox News on Saturday, Whitaker said that Iran had offered "half measures" and "illusory deals to make themselves look good on the world stage"."President Trump's right to reject it," he said.Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Saturday that economic sanctions imposed by the US were taking a toll on Iran.Posting on X, Bessent said Turkey, Oman and the United Arab Emirates had halted flights from various Iranian airlines, and some banks in the UAE and Turkey had stopped transactions with Iran.The Trump administration has dubbed an economic blockade on Iran "Operation Economic Outcast", with the White House attempting to use economic pressure to force Tehran to stop attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.But some economists have questioned whether the latest sanctions will be effective, as this depends on the reaction from Iran's major trading partners.These include China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which has ignored previous US sanctions and continued to do business with Tehran.

schema.headline: Iranian minister says only negotiation can end conflict after Trump rejects Hormuz deal

title: Laver Cup: Carlos Alcaraz saves match points as Team Europe take lead
description: Two-time Wimbledon champion Carlos Alcaraz narrowly avoided back-to-back singles defeats for the first time in 18 months as Team Europe took a 7-5 lea
body: Two-time Wimbledon champion Carlos Alcaraz narrowly avoided back-to-back singles defeats for the first time in 18 months as Team Europe took a 7-5 lead over Team World at the Laver Cup.The world number three saved two match points before overcoming Taylor Fritz 6-3 4-6 13-11 in a dramatic deciding tie-break at London's O2 Arena.It was Alcaraz's first singles outing since his late-night quarter-final exit to Ben Shelton at the US Open."The drop shot is part of my game," Alcaraz said after sealing victory with a trademark touch."In those really close and important moments, I tried to use it because it was a really good weapon for me in this match."American Fritz, whose only previous victory against the Spaniard came during Team World's triumph in last year's competition, kept errors to a minimum.However, Alcaraz struck 42 winners to Fritz's 20, bringing an audience that included Roger Federer and Andy Murray to their feet.Facing match point at 8-9 down in the tie break, Alcaraz fired an ace before leaning on a drop shot to stave off a second. He converted his third match point when Fritz failed to retrieve another delicate drop shot over the net.Earlier on Saturday, Andre Agassi's Team World had threatened to run away with things.Alex de Minaur fought back from a set down to shock Alexander Zverev 2-6 7-6 (7-5) 11-9, while American debutant Learner Tien edged Italy's Flavio Cobolli 6-3 2-6 10-7.Following Alcaraz's singles heroics, Zverev returned to the court alongside Casper Ruud to secure an important 6-4 7-6 (9-7) doubles victory over Alexander Bublik and Brandon Nakashima, keeping Europe ahead going into the final day.Match wins are worth three points on Sunday, with the first team to reach 13 points lifting the trophy.Europe are chasing their sixth Laver Cup title, while holders Team World are aiming for their third.

schema.headline: Laver Cup: Carlos Alcaraz saves match points as Team Europe take lead

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Noel's crying his heart out' and 'global IVF disaster'
description: Many of Sunday's newspapers look ahead to Andy Burnham's first Labour conference as prime minister. The Observer, external describes him as a "people-
body: Many of Sunday's newspapers look ahead to Andy Burnham's first Labour conference as prime minister. The Observer, external describes him as a "people-pleaser with a ruthless streak of ambition." "A skilled communicator praised for his ordinariness," it argues, "will need to bring more clarity to his vision." "Buoyant Burnham is more popular than his party," according to the Sunday Express, external. The Sunday Mirror, external says that losing his father has fuelled his social care mission. The family heartache has spurred him to "grasp the nettle" of reform, it says.The Sunday Times, external writes that ahead of the conference, Chancellor John Healey has raised hopes of help on fuel duty in next month's Budget. The Mail on Sunday , externalbelieves Labour is at war over migrants and the economy, with cabinet ministers trading blows on the eve of the conference.The Sunday Telegraph, external says Burnham is already out of ideas. The country does not need more speeches about "hope," it argues - it needs a prime minister willing to spend political capital forcing change through, whatever the objections of Labour MPs.The Sunday Times , externalsays an estimated 800,000 people greeted the Pope as he travelled down the Champs Elysees in Paris on Sunday. It titles a photo of his visit "Mass appeal." The Sun on Sunday, external headlines its coverage "Chateauneuf-du-Pope.""They think it's all over... it's not" says the Sunday Mirror, external, as it considers the Manchester City's chairman's insistence that - as the Sunday Express, external puts it, the club's "not guilty" of breaching the Premier League's financial rules. The Sunday People, external says one of the club's most famous fans, Noel Gallagher, has insisted the crisis is nothing to do with the players or supporters. The Daily Star Sunday, external reaches for not one, but two Oasis song titles for its coverage. Noel's crying his heart out, it says on page one - while on the back page, suggesting the club chairman is urging people to "Stand by me."The Sunday Times, external says it can finally answer the divisive question of whether you need to rinse cans and jars before recycling them - something, the paper says, has caused marriages to crumble.The head of Britain's biggest recycling firm, Veolia, has told the paper there's no need to rise them out as long as they are "relatively clean." Divorce rates will fall, delights the paper. Except for one nagging question: "What exactly do you mean when you say "relatively."

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Noel's crying his heart out' and 'global IVF disaster'

title: Biao Xiang: Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young Chinese people are anxious about their future in a rapdily changing countryByFan Wang"A star sent from
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young Chinese people are anxious about their future in a rapdily changing countryByFan Wang"A star sent from the heavens," is how Zihan Han describes the man she's become a huge fan of recently, a man who young Chinese people call an "idol".Except this is no pop singer or movie star, but a 54-year old anthropologist. Professor Biao Xiang has become an unlikely guide for an increasingly disillusioned generation.And it's because of what he talks about: anxiety and how to navigate it.China's economy and tech have grown at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z, from jobs to romantic prospects to the sheer pressure of keeping up."The transition from school to the real world brings a lot of uncertainty now, and people often feel anxious because they don't know how to face it," says a 23-year-old Chinese graduate who didn't want to reveal her name because she was worried speaking to foreign media might affect her chances of finding a job back home."People need an anchor in their life. And his words make us feel there is someone that gets me."She and Zihan were among some 500 people - mostly Chinese diaspora - who piled into an auditorium recently in Singapore. Xiang spoke for more than an hour in Mandarin before he took questions. When it ended, dozens queued to meet and take photos with him. The Chinese grad called it "an academic fan meeting".Xiang has been interviewed by major Chinese outlets and has travelled to top Chinese campuses to talk, including at his alma mater, the prestigious Peking University – one talk earlier this year was live-streamed because the auditorium was full.  "When in doubt, ask Biao Xiang," has become a saying, according to Chinese media.Image caption, About 500 people heard Biao Xiang speak in Singapore recentlyIn Sinapore, Xiang spoke of the recognition young people seek in today's China, where they often look to systems for approval - from competitive exams to secure jobs - and how that approval becomes a measure of self-worth, which can be exhausting and damaging. It is healthier, he suggested, to seek meaning and understanding from others and use that to understand ourselves better.These are hardly quick fixes. But in a country where discontent can be politically sensitive and heavily censored, he is a rare public figure who addresses what he calls the "pain point of the times"."Everyone knows where the issue is, but they are reluctant to look at it. Sometimes it is too painful to look at, or they don't have a way," he tells the BBC over tea in Singapore."But as an academic, it is not terrifying if you can describe it – that's how you analyse and manage it."He now lives in Germany, where he is the director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, and studies social change in China and other parts of Asia.Xiang believes Chinese society is at a "turning point", where people are searching for meaning while making sense of rapid social and economic change. He sees contradictions – uncertain youth in a powerful, assertive country; disillusionment despite huge advancement – and his job, he says, is to unpack what is driving it.China's leader Xi Jinping has acknowledged it too: he said the "principal contradiction" was "between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young people are seeking a new narrative in a highly competitive China, Xiang says Xiang has catchy names for what is causing this. "Floating" is how he describes people working relentlessly just to survive, like a hummingbird that keeps flapping its wings to stay mid-air."The nearby" refers to what is immediately around us. Xiang argues that people are preoccupied by the "very near" (themselves) and the very far (the world) while the space in between - "the nearby" - is neglected. This, he says, leaves them feeling disconnected.This seems to be resonating deeply with young people looking for answers. One user on RedNote writes, "He consistently views issues from the perspective of the vulnerable, attributes personal stress to macro-level causes, and encourages people to actively engage with life - it's truly wonderful."Another says, "He never spouts empty, feel-good platitudes; instead, he crouches down to face real-life dilemmas alongside us."Zihan says it boils down to Xiang's willingness to talk openly about these things: "Those who have said similar things aren't as kick-ass as Teacher Xiang, yet people who are as kick-ass as him haven't said such things."Image caption, Xiang has become famous among Chinese people for his candid lecturesBorn in 1972, Xiang came of age during another turning point, as China emerged from the brutal chaos of Mao Zedong's rule to trade with the world. It urbanised, ordinary people turned into entrepreneurs and businesses took off for the first time in the Communist nation.Growing up in Wenzhou, which transformed into an industrial port, Xiang witnessed this first-hand. "It was a vast landscape of small business owners," he recalls. "Most people didn't care too much about education, the focus was on practical matters - specifically, how to make money."And many of them did. Their children grew up in a glorious era of double-digit economic growth. But the economy slowed during Covid and hasn't bounced back. The old equation - hard work = secure job - no longer works, and they want a new narrative, Xiang says.Youth unemployment hit 21.3%, before the government stopped publishing the data in mid-2023. Those with "good jobs" - civil servants, corporate employees, engineers - are anxious about losing them.They constantly complain online about long, exhausting working hours and a toxic office culture and their fear of the "curse of 35" - a cutoff age for job advertisements, after which it is harder to find a new job.Because of censorship, it's hard to know the true extent of this mood. But that feeling of being squeezed seeps into public discourse in other ways. That anxiety quickly turns into anger in online debates, be it about university entrance exams or bride price or food safety scandals.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young people praying at monastery in Beijing for bright job and marriage prospects   Terms associated with this mood have been trending for years. The most famous are "lying flat", when people opt out of the rat race entirely, and "involution", a rather clunky term now commonly used to describe intense competition which generates little meaningful reward.Xiang believes two forces have amplified this anxiety - the property market and the higher education system. The property boom, fuelled by local government's reliance on land sales, tied families' sense of security and success to the values of their homes. And a rapid expansion in university enrolment raised the bar for achievement, intensifying competition.The result, he says, is a universal playbook: get a good degree, find a stable job, marry and buy a home."When 1.4 billion people are all in the same race, that is involution."About three years ago, when he learned that a camp for digital nomads where he spoke raised prices after his visit, he "realised I was no longer only known in the academic circles".Many of his peers, he said, prioritise publishing research and are "quite cold" to his methods. Some warned him about "cherishing your feathers", a Chinese expression for protecting one's reputation.But Xiang is encouraged by his popularity."If someone calls me an influencer I'll take it as a compliment. Because the real influence I can have is to make people think for themselves."

schema.headline: Biao Xiang: Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety

title: Why some charity shop donations do more harm than good
description: Jane Ward is turning the blackened, mouldy pages of a Mr Men book. "You wouldn't want your child curled up in bed with this," she says.We are at a cha
body: Jane Ward is turning the blackened, mouldy pages of a Mr Men book. "You wouldn't want your child curled up in bed with this," she says.We are at a charity shop run by St Barnabas Hospice in Lincoln. On the table in front of us is a fleece work jacket, covered in dog hair, along with a large, stained teddy bear and a single, dirty, grey slipper."If we had the pair, it still wouldn't be wearable," Ward, the store's deputy manager, tells me. "Even our rag companies wouldn't be able to accept that."Broken, dirty and downright grotty donations are costing hospice charities tens of thousands of pounds to dispose of.St Barnabas and Dove House Hospice, in Hull, spent a combined £70,000 on dealing with unwanted waste last year.While St Barnabas says the quality of donations can be "phenomenal", staff are calling on people to be more mindful of items the charity will not be able to sell and which instead become a cost.Its flagship shop, called The Warehouse, is a large unit on an industrial estate with a retail space out front, selling furniture, electrical goods, homeware and toys, as well as racks of clothing and shoes.According to the hospice website, the store has generated more than £2m in income since opening in 2022. But some donations cost the charity money. In the back room, where the sorting happens, Ward picks out items that will never make the shelves."These teddies don't have the CE safety mark and they're also very dirty," she says, before showing me a toddler's wooden jigsaw. "The game has pieces missing – it's unsellable."Caroline Peach is the hospice's head of retail, overseeing 23 shops across Lincolnshire. She stresses that the charity relies on donations, but says they are also getting rid of huge amounts of people's stuff. Last year, they recycled 350 tonnes.Then there are the items that simply have to be binned."We do incur waste costs for the stuff we just can't sell, stuff that our recycling merchants can't accept, broken crockery, toys that are missing parts, that kind of thing."Last year, we spent £30,000 on waste disposal just across our shops."I think the public are very aware of being sustainable, not putting stuff into landfill. And so, they immediately think, I'll support my local charity. But they need to be mindful of the things that the charity can't sell, that then become a cost."Both hospice charities have online lists to explain what they can and cannot take.They have examples to share of what makes a great donation.Good quality homewares do well.Ward holds up a saucepan. "It's been used but it's still perfectly clean. Here's a lovely mug with no tea stains.""Not wine glasses," she adds. "They are so cheap in the supermarkets, we just can't sell them.Rowan shows a pair of shoes, hardly worn and from an expensive high street store."These will fly off the shelves, they're in beautiful condition," she beams."I always think a good way to look at it is, 'Would you buy it yourself?' If the answer is 'yes', then we will happily take your items."Download the BBC News app from the App Store, external for iPhone and iPad or Google Play, external for Android devices

schema.headline: Why some charity shop donations do more harm than good

title: Time running out for Tennessee killer Christa Pike who says she's too damaged for death row
description: Killer Christa Pike is to be executed within days - but her defence say she's a victim tooImage source, Tennesse Department of CorrectionsImage captio
body: Killer Christa Pike is to be executed within days - but her defence say she's a victim tooImage source, Tennesse Department of CorrectionsImage caption, Christa Pike's lawyers have filed a clemency petition seeking to commute her sentence ahead of the 30 September execution date ByStephanie HegartyBBC World Service CorrespondentAshlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee.Pike told Sellars she does not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed. "She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says.Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago.Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995 when Colleen was found with a pentagram, a symbol of Satanic ritual, carved into her chest.Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set for Wednesday. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting".Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Student Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed in the 1995 murderBut Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, and UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped., external Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider."It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence."Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness."Image source, Christa PikeImage caption, Christa Pike suffered neglect and was abused by her parentsIn 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened.But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged more than a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge.In 2021 Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since.Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her."Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual, and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says.Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation."Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable."Image source, Christa PikeImage caption, Pike, pictured as a teenager, killed Slemmer in January 1995 after telling a friend she "just felt mean that day", court documents say'She should pay for it'Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution.A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father, and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD, and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict. The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy.Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence, and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021.Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment, and Lee has never granted clemency in a death penalty case before.The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps.On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it.Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution."She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she said on Knoxville TV station WBIR in 2021, and told the BBC this week she still stands by those comments.Pike should suffer before she dies, Martinez told WBIR. "I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did."Image source, J. Miles Carey/USA TODAY/Imagn Images via ReutersImage caption, May Martinez, mother of Colleen Slemmer, and a retired Knoxville Police department detective outside a courtroom for a post-conviction hearing in 2006"My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added."There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting."The Justice Coalition, a victims' rights advocacy group, has raised money to help Martinez travel to Tennessee to watch the execution.The group's executive director, Robert Bracewell, said this sentence was determined by a jury of Pike's peers and it is what Colleen's family want."We stand firm with the family that on the 30 September her execution ought to proceed."Ashlee Sellars grapples with two seemingly conflicting beliefs: that Colleen's mother has a right to feel justice has been served and that everyone, including her friend Christa, deserves a chance at redemption."When I think about reconciling who you see on TV or the horrible tragedy that happened with Colleen, the only thing that makes sense to me is around mental health and trauma and the way that people process stuff in a moment when they don't have the things that they need," Sellars says."These horrible things happen in your youth and then those traumas moved through you, in our community, and you cause harm to somebody else."Sellars met Pike in prison while serving a 25-year sentence for her involvement in a robbery-murder. They spoke to each other through the meal flaps in their doors on the high security unit. Now, Sellars works as an advocate for justice reform and victims of crime."People want to know that everyone's life matters, right? They want to know that Colleen's life mattered," she says."Christa in this moment, I think she is fighting much more for her life to matter than she is to actually live."

schema.headline: Time running out for Tennessee killer Christa Pike who says she's too damaged for death row

title: Pickford or Trafford? Has the battle to be England's number one started?
description: You have to go back 10 years to find a major tournament where Jordan Pickford was not starting in goal for England. The Everton goalkeeper has pretty
body: You have to go back 10 years to find a major tournament where Jordan Pickford was not starting in goal for England. The Everton goalkeeper has pretty much been England's number one since making his debut in 2017 - until now.Saturday's 3-2 Nations League loss to Spain saw Leeds' James Trafford make his competitive debut for the Three Lions as manager Thomas Tuchel signalled the battle to be number one is on.Pickford became England's highest appearance maker at World Cups, overtaking Peter Shilton when he started in England's 2026 quarter-final win over Norway.During Gareth Southgate's tenure there was not a natural goalkeeper to rival Pickford, and that looked to continue under Tuchel as Pickford started all but one of England's World Cup qualifiers and then every game in the summer. But it looks as though Pickford has finally got a rival in Trafford, with Tuchel saying that the pair get "two consecutive matches each" during this international break.Trafford has impressed since making his move to Leeds for a deal worth up to £45m.Against Spain, the 23-year-old showed his quality with the ball at his feet and made an impressive save to deny Ferran Torres in the first half. But he was beaten three times as England lost their Nations League opener to the world champions."I think he deserved to get the two matches, that's why we gave him two matches," Tuchel said."He started the Premier League season well and gets minutes as number one at Leeds."Jordan [Pickford] did absolutely nothing wrong but we wanted to use this competition to see how far actually James is."Trafford's form this season has helped Leeds to fifth in the Premier League table.He has kept two clean sheets and now has his chance to stake his claim as England's future number one over two matches. Trafford had only played 32 top-flight games before moving to Leeds following time at Burnley and Manchester City. He came through City's academy and joined Burnley for an initial fee of £15m in the summer of 2023.However, he conceded 67 goals in only 28 matches before losing his place towards the end of the 2023-24 season.But after starring in Burnley's successful promotion in 2024-25 and the Clarets conceding just 16 goals, Trafford returned to City for £27m last summer with the hope of being Pep Guardiola's number one.City brought in one of the best goalkeepers in the world in Gianluigi Donnarumma, just four weeks after Trafford's arrival and he became second choice. Despite it being a frustrating campaign, Trafford did get vital experience and started both the FA Cup final and Carabao Cup final for City before his move to Leeds. He has been part of England success too, winning the U21 European Championship in 2023 and saving a stoppage-time penalty as Lee Carsley's side beat Spain in the final.

schema.headline: Pickford or Trafford? Has the battle to be England's number one started?

title: Can you be healthy if you eat ultra-processed foods? I asked a dietitian
description: Can you eat ultra-processed foods and still be healthy? A dietitian analysed my weekly shopImage source, Getty ImagesByRuth CleggHealth and wellbeing
body: Can you eat ultra-processed foods and still be healthy? A dietitian analysed my weekly shopImage source, Getty ImagesByRuth CleggHealth and wellbeing reporterGoing to the supermarket has become a minefield.I'm in aisle 15, reading long lists of ingredients and worrying if what's in my trolley is good for me or not.There's growing evidence, external that a hefty proportion of the food we consume could be damaging to our health, with ultra-processed foods (UPFs) linked to a range of health problems.But I've had enough of second-guessing myself and panicking I'm poisoning my child if I feed him chicken nuggets, so I've given my shopping list to a dietitian to analyse.Image caption, Even the most chemical-sounding ingredients in chicken nuggets are tested and approved under UK food lawsFirst things first, what is a UPF?It depends who you ask. A basic rule of thumb is that to be ultra-processed a product needs more than five ingredients, with at least one not normally found in your kitchen - things like emulsifiers, additives and flavourings.There is a large and growing body of evidence that shows UPFs are linked to obesity, cardiovascular disease and metabolic disorders such as diabetes, as well as mental health problems and even premature death.But scientists, doctors and dietitians can't agree on why. Is it purely down to the high fat, sugar, salt and calorie content? Or is the ultra-processing also a factor?Studies show more than half the calories we consume in the UK come from ultra-processed food, external. Dr Chris van Tulleken has written books and made documentaries about how bad these foods can be, and he tells me they're "almost impossible to avoid" - even his own family's diet includes a few.And my shopping list isn't UPF-free either.Maeve Hanan, a member of the British Dietetic Association, pauses as she scans through some of my weekly shopping list (there was more fruit and veg, honest) and points to a box of bran flakes."This is ultra-processed, but I often buy this for my family. It's got so many health benefits."Hanan says there's a "growing hysteria" about UPFs."Mainly because the messaging around them is so black and white," she says. "This food is good. This food is bad. "It just fuels fear - and fear around food is never good."Image caption, A snapshot of my shopping list So what is her verdict on my grocery shopping? Not as bad as I expected, I'm relieved to learn. While there are UPFs in there, that doesn't necessarily make it an unhealthy food shop. In fact, Hanan says, "there's a good mix of foods which cover each food group".Just because some products have a long ingredient list, it doesn't make them "inherently bad", she explains, with the nutritional value "far more important".What about foods that contain ingredients I can barely pronounce, never mind recognise? Hanan takes my son's chicken nuggets as an example."There are mandatory vitamins and minerals which manufacturers in the UK are required to add to white wheat flour such as calcium carbonate, niacin and thiamin," she says.Raising agents, such as disodium diphosphate, are used alongside sodium bicarbonate (baking powder) to make the batter crisp and light.Hanan says even the most chemical-sounding ingredients will have been tested and approved under UK food laws."But while chicken nuggets are a good source of protein," she warns, "they are higher in fat and salt than a plain chicken breast, so I would eat them in moderation as part of a balanced diet."I tell Hanan my son usually eats them with raw carrot sticks and pasta."One food does not make your diet healthy or unhealthy," she says, "it's about getting that balance over time."Megan Bamford believes cutting out UPFs from her diet has helped her manage irritable bowel syndrome and chronic pain.But now, as a mum to two young children, cooking from scratch is not always viable. Her eldest, seven-year-old Ella, has struggled on and off with food since she was little."It's not always easy to feed your children what you think they should eat," Megan says. "Ella has been poorly in the past because of her severe picky eating - we had no choice but to give her ultra-processed food from a packet."Image source, Megan BamfordImage caption, Megan cut out ultra-processed foods to help manage her health, but focuses on choosing the healthiest options available for her childrenSo Megan's kitchen is still full of fruit, vegetables, seeds and oats but there are now also breakfast cereals, crisps, biscuits and other processed foods too.She looks for food with five ingredients or fewer. "Most of the snacks, pizzas, and cereal I buy are not ultra-processed," she says. "I'm happy with that. I feed my children in the best way I can, I choose the healthiest options I can find."While many UPFs are high in fat, sugar and salt, which we know cause a whole range of health problems, some scientists say there is not as much understanding about what the act of processing does to our food.Author and food scientist Prof David Julian McClements says the "ultra-processed food idea is not very well defined"."Focussing on the processing element is a bit of red herring," he says, "I don't think that's the main problem here."Some studies suggest, external the more processed food is, the easier it is to overeat it. Others link UPFs to changes in our gut microbiome. But McClements says there is no conclusive evidence to say this alone inherently damages our health.But given he works in the food industry, does he have a vested interest?"Any successful food scientist works a lot with the food industry," McClements says, "and I think trying to get rid of UPFs is holding back innovation."So many of us lead busy lives, he says, convenience is a major part of society."What I want to do is to redesign processed foods to make them healthier," he says.Image caption, Experts are calling for clearer labelling of ultra-processed cereals high in fat, sugar and saltWhen I put this to van Tulleken he pauses for breath. He's just been highlighting the high sugar content in various breakfast cereals while waving an empty box of a very sugary and chocolatey one at me. I feel a pang of guilt, knowing my seven-year-old son can get through several bowls in a single sitting."UPFs are tasty, they are moreish - that's the whole point," van Tulleken says. "Of course, we can make UPFs healthier - but then they're not as nice."The food companies know very well how to make healthy food. The reason they don't is because it's not profitable."He says there's growing evidence which shows industrial processing does affect our health and that businesses control the food market in a way that is "very harmful"."What we need for starters is better food labelling so we know which foods have high fat, sugar and salt content which we know is bad for us - and that makes up the majority of UPFs."The Food and Drink Federation, which represents food and drink manufacturers in the UK, strongly disagrees with van Tulleken's claims. It says it has invested millions of pounds "in healthier product innovation" and its members have "cut the salt, sugar and calories from their products by almost a fifth just in the last five years"."This work," it says, "has been done in line with government regulation and dietary guidance, which focusses on the nutritional content of food rather than the level of processing."So as I slide four chicken nuggets on to my son's dinner plate - alongside his carrots and pasta - I'm not feeling the usual shame and panic. He's an active little boy, he doesn't have nuggets every night, and he's eaten from a range of food groups through the day.He gives me a grin. "This is the best tea ever, Mummy," he says.One day I'm sure he will eat less beige food, but, for now, he's healthy (I hope) and happy.

schema.headline: Can you be healthy if you eat ultra-processed foods? I asked a dietitian

title: Dog rescued from cliff at Pecca Falls in Ingleton
description: A dog stranded on a narrow ledge at the bottom of a 40ft (12m) cliff next to a waterfall has been safely retrieved thanks to the efforts of a voluntee
body: A dog stranded on a narrow ledge at the bottom of a 40ft (12m) cliff next to a waterfall has been safely retrieved thanks to the efforts of a volunteer-run rescue team.Yorkshire Dales charity Cave Rescue Organisation (CRO) and North Yorkshire Fire and Rescue responded to the incident at the well-known Pecca Falls, in Ingleton, after 15:15 BST on Saturday.Eight-year-old Labrador Penny had fallen into the river before becoming stuck after climbing up to a rocky outcrop 6.5ft (2m) above the water. Using a rope system, a volunteer was lowered to the ledge to reach the dog before she was "hauled back up the gorge where she was reunited with her owners".The fire service's Ripon swiftwater rescue team provided support downstream from where Penny was stranded.

schema.headline: Dog rescued from cliff at Pecca Falls in Ingleton

title: Suffolk and Essex NHS remove 10 staff over Noah Woods data breach
description: Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Noah's family paid tribute to a "happy, cheeky, playful" boyByTom McArthur and Louise ParryUpdated 1 hour a
body: Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Noah's family paid tribute to a "happy, cheeky, playful" boyByTom McArthur and Louise ParryUpdated 1 hour agoTen NHS staff have been removed from duty or suspended after a data breach involving the digital medical records of three-year-old Noah Woods.Launching an "urgent" investigation, Dr Martin Mansfield, deputy chief medical officer at East Suffolk and North Essex NHS Foundation Trust, said that any unauthorised access of patient data was "completely unacceptable".The trust has apologised "unreservedly" to Noah's family and said disciplinary action would be taken if needed.A major search for Noah was carried out in the village of Brantham, Suffolk, after the child went missing on 15 September. His body was found the next day in nearby water by police divers.A spokesperson for the trust said 10 employees had been "removed from active duty or suspended whilst investigations are concluded".'Swift action'In the statement issued on Sunday,, external Mansfield said: "Immediate steps were also taken to secure the records and prevent further access that was not for a legitimate, clinical reason."We have reported the matter to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), and we will continue to keep Noah's family informed as our investigation progresses."Anna Turner, the trust's deputy director of communications, said the breaches were found through a "proactive" search because the case was high profile.She said the trust was taking steps to prevent further unlawful access to records."We've made it impossible to find [Noah's] record, which is something we're able to do in this specific case," she added. On Saturday, the trust wrote to all staff informing them about the breach and "to make it clear we're taking very swift action"."We train all of our staff on information governance practice, with regular reminders, including posters in staff areas," Turner added.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Police said at least 1,300 members of the public had joined emergency services in the search for the missing boyAt least 1,300 people helped in the search for Noah in the 24 hours before he was found.A tribute issued by his family called him a "happy, cheeky, playful" boy who loved to laugh. His mother urged other parents to "hold their children a little tighter and cherish every moment".An inquest, which opened on Friday, heard that the three-year-old had left a play area "through a gap in the fence".Assistant coroner Jyoti Gill said it was a "very sad and tragic death" as she opened and adjourned the inquest in Ipswich.If you, or someone you know, have been affected by child bereavement, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action LineGet in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Suffolk and Essex NHS remove 10 staff over Noah Woods data breach

title: Fresh bedsheets and dusk walks: Experts' sleep tips for freshers
description: Image source, Anna-May DixonImage caption, Twenty-year-old Anna-May manages on about five hours' sleep a nightByPhilippa RoxbyHealth reporterIt's the
body: Image source, Anna-May DixonImage caption, Twenty-year-old Anna-May manages on about five hours' sleep a nightByPhilippa RoxbyHealth reporterIt's the start of university - you're already on your fourth themed night out of the week and have signed up for every quirky-sounding society your campus has to offer. But your relationship with your bed could be key to keeping up with a busy social life, as well as that lengthy reading list."If you can get out before 11am-ish then there's a part of the brain, just behind the eyes, that responds to light," says Jo Baker, a psychotherapist and student sleep and mental health expert."Getting daylight early on in the day is really going to help to keep your body in check. How you sleep at night starts with how you wake up in the morning."Sleep is essential to learning and absorbing information. But late nights out, noisy flatmates and a strange new bed can mean good sleep habits go out the window.Image source, Anna-May DixonImage caption, She tries to stay awake during her commute to uni but admits sometimes "dosing off a bit"For Anna-May, 20, it's her four-hour round trip from Kendal, Cumbria to study dance at the University of Salford that leaves her short of sleep. She gets about five hours a night - the alarm goes at 05:00."I track my sleep and get worried about how little I will get, and then sometimes that keeps me up," she says. "I can tell I'm more tired towards the end of the week and things can feel harder."Forcing yourself to have an early night isn't going to work, according to Baker, especially if you end up lying wide awake in bed."Your brain learns this is somewhere I lie and get stressed about not being able to sleep - so the most important thing is a consistent waking time," she says.Alcohol and caffeine don't helpWhen you feel groggy, it's tempting to chug multiple coffees or fizzy drinks. But caffeine hangs around in the body and blocks the build-up of sleepiness throughout the day. Too many flat whites and you'll not only be short of cash - you could also develop a sleep problem.Alcohol may also be a tempting way to boost your confidence around new people, but it doesn't help you sleep. "When you fall asleep [after large amounts of alcohol], you're anaesthetised really. It's like having an anaesthetic. You're not asleep," Baker says.In fact, alcohol pushes out the deep sleep which restores you physically, and replaces it with lighter sleep, which doesn't.Emma Young, deputy director of student services for health and wellbeing at Manchester Metropolitan University points out the low-key alternatives during freshers' week."There are lots of alcohol-free events now, like sip and paint. You can also try wellness and wellbeing clubs, like yoga and crafts, if you don't fancy the sport or music societies."Switch off properly before sleepAnna-May likes a hot shower or bath before bed, which research suggests helps the body's core temperature to cool down and prepare for sleep.Then the only way she can get to sleep is to watch episodes of Friends on her iPad."I watch something I have seen time and time again - it's enough to quieten the busy part of my mind and I can fall to sleep," she says.Image source, Elly WelfordImage caption, Anna-May, who is studying dance, accepts that watching TV before bed goes "against all the advice"But activities without screens like journalling or reading a book might be best for creating a calm, gradual transition to sleep. Listening to music or a podcast can also work.The natural hormone melatonin rises before bedtime, making us feel sleepy. But watching social media reels or films means your eyes stay active, blocking that process and keeping you awake.Baker also suggests: Switching off screens an hour and a half before bed Avoiding a heavy meal just before going to bedWashing your sheets so they are nice and clean to get intoChucking a throw over your laptop, books and desk so you know work is done for the dayGoing for a walk at dusk - the changing light is a signal to the brainKeeping your bed for sleeping in (rather than eating, working or watching YouTube)Image source, Joanna BakerImage caption, Student sleep expert Jo Baker says making your bed in the morning can help signal that sleep is overPlan for feeling ill in bedFeeling unwell can of course impact your sleep patterns.Freshers' flu is tricky to avoid, but good hand hygiene - washing regularly or using antibacterial hand gel - might just reduce your chances of getting a fever, sore throat and blocked nose, and spending a day or two in bed.Meningitis is far more dangerous and requires urgent medical help (call 999). It can look a lot like freshers' flu but if it's not diagnosed, it can progress very quickly and lead to seizures, brain damage and sepsis. That's why a free NHS vaccine called Men B is now on offer to all freshers students.Many universities recommend planning ahead in case you feel ill and need some medical help at some point, especially if you're living away from home.A typical to-do list should include:Registering with a local GPFinding your nearest chemistRegistering with an NHS dentistFinding out where the closest A&E isYou might also want to check out what your uni has to offer in terms of mental health support. Some pair up students for peer support and run dedicated 24-hour phone lines.Websites like Student Minds, external have lots of useful advice and information.And if you're not feeling like yourself, Young suggests a regular call home, to family or a best friend.Get in touchHave you been affected by issues covered in this story?  Share your experiences.

schema.headline: Fresh bedsheets and dusk walks: Experts' sleep tips for freshers

title: Hummingbird hawk moths and ivy bees: The insects growing in number as temperatures rise
description: Image source, Getty Images/Gregory DubusImage caption, The hummingbird hawk moth hovers as it feeds from flowers, much like its feathered namesakeBySh
body: Image source, Getty Images/Gregory DubusImage caption, The hummingbird hawk moth hovers as it feeds from flowers, much like its feathered namesakeByShehnaz KhanWest MidlandsAs parts of the West Midlands baked in warmer temperatures this summer, species once considered unusual in the region, such as hummingbird hawk moths, ivy bees and the wasp spider have been spotted in growing numbers.The hummingbird hawk moth, known for its furry grey body, orange hindwings and long proboscis, migrates to the UK from southern Europe and north Africa in the summer months. James Benwell, from the Birmingham and Black Country Wildlife Trust, said 2026 was a "record year" for sightings of the species, which was often mistaken for a small bird.The moth, which can be seen hovering over flowers, has wings that beat about 80 times per second, external, according to Benwell."They've had a really good year this year," he said. "Normally they would come in small numbers. We'd normally hear of a few maybe. But this year, we've seen loads of records of them."They're absolutely amazing but I somehow haven't seen one this year, so I'm jealous of anybody else that has."Image source, Getty Images/Finnbarr WebsterImage caption, The moth migrates to the UK from southern Europe and north Africa in the summer monthsIvy bees, which feed mainly on the nectar of ivy flowers, had also become more prevalent in the Midlands, Benwell said, adding they were easy to find on buildings.The bees, first recorded in the UK in 2001, are slowly spreading north, after first being recorded in the region in Stourbridge in 2015."There's nothing that distinguishes them from other bees really, they're not that kind of attention-grabbing species, but, you know, were you to look for them, go to ivy and you'll see them," Benwell said.Image source, Getty Images/Image Broker/Kevin SawfordImage caption, The ivy bee was first recorded on British shores in 2001Other insects that had seen an increase in their numbers locally included the clouded yellow butterfly, a European migratory species known to have "peak" years during unusually hot summers."Most individuals are unable to survive the British winter, but if temperatures continue to rise as a result of climate change, we may well see them becoming permanent residents," Benwell said."There's numerous species that we could point out that weren't here 20 years ago... and now they're quite abundant."Image source, Getty Images/Sandra StandbridgeImage caption, The clouded yellow butterfly was a regular visitor to Britain and Ireland, the Butterfly Conservation saidOthers once more commonly associated with southern England have also spread further north.The trust said the hornet hoverfly, with yellow markings that mimic a hornet to protect against predators, although it cannot sting, had become really common after it was first recorded in Birmingham and the Black Country in 2004.Another species, the cricket bat spider, which gets its name from its cricket bat-like markings, has also become more common in grassland since it was first spotted in the region in 2019.The sightings come as one of the UK's largest spider species, the wasp spider, was spotted in the Midlands as warmer temperatures pushed it more than 100 miles away from its usual habitat.The spider has recently been recorded in Worcestershire, alongside sightings in Herefordshire and Warwickshire, said the Worcestershire Wildlife Trust.Image source, Wendy CarterImage caption, The wasp spider is known for its distinctive yellow, black and white stripesRosemary Winnall, from the Wyre Forest Study Group, which maps the wildlife and ecology of the forest in Worcestershire, said the arrival of the wasp spider was to be celebrated.She said the group was always on the lookout for new arrivals and had already recorded the willow emerald damselfly, the southern oak bush cricket and the purple emperor butterfly, as more species travelled north."The impressive western conifer seed bug is here as is the box bug," she added.Hot weather had also benefited butterflies that loved sunshine, such as the holly blue and the pearl-bordered fritillary, which the Butterfly Conservation charity, external said was once "very widespread" but had rapidly declined in recent decades.However, despite an increase in some species appearing in the region, there were others whose numbers were dwindling."The once-common small tortoiseshell butterfly is now rarely seen for example, and there are far fewer records of the two-spot ladybird," Winnall explained."We are encouraging folk to record the common species of today as they may be the rarities of the future."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Birmingham and the Black Country

schema.headline: Hummingbird hawk moths and ivy bees: The insects growing in number as temperatures rise

title: Scotland: From turgid to thrusting - mixed start for new Scotland
description: Figure caption, Highlights: Slovenia 0-0 ScotlandByBBC Scotland's chief sports writerFor 45 turgid minutes in Slovenia, some in the Tartan Army might
body: Figure caption, Highlights: Slovenia 0-0 ScotlandByBBC Scotland's chief sports writerFor 45 turgid minutes in Slovenia, some in the Tartan Army might have reimagined the Steve Clarke years as a time of plenty, the halcyon era of ambitious football when Scotland were an all-electric thrill-fest.The opening half of the Sebastien Pocognoli regime was, as expected, disjointed. It was also, rather unexpectedly, devoid of anything remotely related to what Pocognoli laid out as his non-negotiables - front-foot pressing, high intensity, speed of thought and mind, goal threat.They had no shot on target and lost so many aerial duels that you stopped counting beyond the half-hour mark. They took 38 minutes to touch the ball in Slovenia's penalty area.It wasn't like they were under major pressure - the hosts are a pretty toothless side  - but neither were they accurate or energetic. Everybody who preached patience in the new era gulped hard. This was not good. We didn't expect champagne, but this was stale beer.And then it changed, not so completely that Scotland roared and won the game, but they certainly cleared their throats as an attacking force.McBurnie and co show promise without poiseFrom being impotent, they became thrusting. That second half was as big a 0-0 rout as you're likely to see. Frustrating, but encouraging at the same time.It will be agonising for Oli McBurnie that he's still without an international goal - he said he wouldn't sleep after failing to convert a one-on-one with Jan Oblak - but his second-half performance was full of good things; efforts on goal, link-up play, presence and danger. Robbie Ure hit a post, Kieron Bowie had a terrific chance, but missed. The three strikers drew a blank, but as far as 0-0s go, it offered hope that more productive days may lay ahead with these guys.There are two ways of looking at the draw. All 10 starting outfield players had a shot on goal, the first time that's happened since June 2022, against Armenia. Scotland had 17 shots, their most attempts in a competitive game in more than 14 years. The flipside is that they have now failed to score in three tournament games in a row for the first time in almost 22 years.After the break, Pocognoli dropped McBurnie a little deeper, in a pocket just behind Robbie Ure and then Bowie when he came on. He got Billy Gilmour to sit lower in midfield, where he had time to dictate, which he absolutely did. Gilmour tied it all together in the second half.Pocognoli called it "two games in one game" and he was right. The subtle shift in McBurnie's and Gilmour's positioning brought Scotland alive. It was an impressive watch; ambition, relentlessness, belief. No cherry on top but enough there to leave most folk happy about day one and motivated ahead of day two, against Switzerland on Tuesday night at Hampden.Figure caption, 'I'm not going to be able to sleep thinking about those chances' - McBurnieMcBurnie, not so much the prodigal son but now the forgiven one, had that big chance six minutes into the new half - the one he would have dreamed about. He created it for himself, winning possession and getting into a wonderful position right in front of an isolated Oblak.He could have dinked it as the goalkeeper committed himself, he could have slid it home to Oblak's left or through his legs. Instead, he went for the flourish, trying to take it round the Slovenian and marking his return to the side after 2,005 days in the wilderness with a first goal on his 17th appearance.Oblak won the duel. Painful, for sure, but a prelude to a stirring second half from the striker and his new-old team-mates. McBurnie played a slick one-two with the increasingly dominant Gilmour, who had his shot saved. Oblak was by a million miles Slovenia's best player.McBurnie had a header fly over, Aaron Hickey had a header just wide, Bowie came on and had an immediate impact. He had three chances in eight minutes - a tame shot, a clipped attempt and then the big one - played in by Gilmour but pulled wide. In that moment, he joined McBurnie and Ure (after hitting a post late in the first half) in the torture chamber.In the midst of all of that, McBurnie powered a header on goal, but Oblak was equal to it. That was Scotland's ninth consecutive crack without reply. They were utterly dominant but achingly goalless. So much encouraging stuff and yet just one point to show for it when it really should have been three.Pocognoli demonstrates tactical acumenPocognoli said he was heartened by that second half. Scotland fans should be buoyed by the new head coach recognising the problems in his team and then fixing them. With such a small track record to feed off, the subject of his tactical acumen was always going to be an interesting one - the ownership of the second 45 minutes showed that he's no slouch in identifying and changing the things that need to be changed.Going with McBurnie and Ure up front was something of a surprise, but it sent a signal out that Scotland are here to go on the offensive rather than just defend their way to decent outcomes.That didn't materialise in the first half, but it clicked in the second. It's a touch surreal that, at the end of another game when Scotland failed to score, there is a lot to be hopeful about in the men who are there to supply the goals.McBurnie, Ure and Bowie are an exciting trio. When others are fit, there's Che Adams, Lawrence Shankland, Tommy Conway and Ross Stewart. Young James Wilson will have his moment at some point. New blood has joined the old guard and things should be better when everything settles down.For Pocognoli, the next test is the biggest one. Switzerland, ranked 14th in the world, are missing some serious operators, but they are brilliantly coached by Murat Yakin and they're settled and formidable. Their whole is greater than the sum of their parts. This will be a fascinating examination of Pocognoli's prowess. Win on Tuesday night and it's lift-off time.Figure caption, 'The second half was complete dominance' - Halliday on Pocognoli's debut

schema.headline: Scotland: From turgid to thrusting - mixed start for new Scotland
